title: AI in the Classroom
author: Aneesh Sohoni
summary: Sohoni introduces a Top Five list from Emily Freitag of Instruction Partners, whose team studied 20 AI-powered instructional products and observed them in real classrooms. The central argument is that AI in schools brings real opportunities and real challenges, and that both depend on the choices educators make about how tools enter the learning experience. Opportunities include individualized feedback, an easier teaching job, and better support for multilingual learners. Challenges include damaging shortcuts from general-purpose chatbots and uneven implementation. The framing move contrasts general chatbots that let students shortcut thinking with targeted instructional tools designed to deepen it, while keeping teacher judgment central.
points: Instruction Partners studied 20 AI instructional products and went into classrooms to see what actually happened when teachers and students used them.
AI can give individualized feedback to 25 or more students at once, notably on writing, increasing both volume and speed of feedback.
General-purpose chatbots make it easy for students to copy answers, which undermines the effort that learning requires.
Implementation conditions such as schedule time and a clear vision for teacher action mediate whether a product has any impact.
Translation features help multilingual learners access grade-level content in their home languages while teachers remain central.
quotes: They studied 20 AI-powered instructional products and went into classrooms to see what actually happened when teachers and students used them.
While general-purpose chatbots can make it easier for students to shortcut the thinking learning requires, targeted instructional tools can be designed to deepen it.
Many AI-powered products have the capacity to tailor feedback to individual students, addressing 25+ specific needs, simultaneously.

Learning anything requires effort, and products that intentionally or unintentionally reduce the thinking that students need to do to complete their assignments will unquestionably undermine learning.

Nothing I’ve seen on this tour makes me think that teachers will be any less central to driving teaching and learning than they’ve always been, but what I did see suggests that supporting key moves will require far fewer heroics than it has historically.
Across the tour, we saw students experience the same products, even the same activities, quite differently, classroom to classroom.

As a sector, we must remember that product design ratings and the evidence of impact that a given product has will never tell the whole story—implementation will always mediate a product’s impact on student learning.
